Finding the rows that match a condition, such as all orders for one customer.

before.note: Read Databases and Sharding first: an index speeds lookups within a database, and search spreads indexes across shards. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Without help, finding rows that match a condition means reading every row, a full table scan, which gets slow as the table grows. An index is a separate, ordered structure the database keeps alongside the data so it can jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning them all. It is the same idea as the index at the back of a book [[pg-indexes-intro]].

An index trades space and write cost for read speed. It takes extra storage, and every insert or update must also update the index, so writes get a little slower. In return, the right query becomes dramatically faster. Deciding which indexes to keep is a balance between faster reads and slower, larger writes [[pg-indexes-intro]].

Search engines generalise the same idea to text. Instead of scanning every document for a word, they build an inverted index that maps each word to the list of documents containing it, so a search jumps straight to the matching documents. Lucene, the engine behind many search systems, is built around this structure [[lucene]].

terms.definition: An ordered structure beside the data that lets the database find matching rows without scanning all of them.
Reading every row to answer a query, the slow fallback when no index helps.
A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, the core of text search.
How few rows a condition matches; an index helps most when a query is selective.
The extra write work indexes add, since each must be updated on every change.

stages.name: How it works
body: The default index type in most databases is the B-tree, a balanced tree that keeps keys in sorted order. It answers equality lookups and range queries efficiently because the sort order lets the database descend to a key and then walk neighbours. PostgreSQL uses B-tree by default and also offers hash, GIN, GiST and others for specific needs [[pg-indexes-types]].

The index type must match the query. A hash index serves equality but not ranges. A GIN index suits values that contain many items, such as the words in a document or the keys in a JSON field, which is how a relational database does its own full-text search. Choosing the type is choosing which queries get fast [[pg-indexes-types]].

Text search needs more than exact matching. Before building the inverted index, the engine breaks text into tokens, lowercases them, and often reduces words to a root form so that run, runs and running match. This analysis step decides what a search can and cannot find, and it happens both when indexing and when querying [[es-docs]].

A relevant point for scale: in a search system each shard holds its own inverted index over its share of the documents, so a query runs on every shard in parallel and the results are merged and ranked. Elasticsearch builds directly on this, with indices split into shards across nodes [[es-docs]].

terms.definition: A balanced, sorted tree index that serves both equality and range queries efficiently.
An index that answers equality lookups quickly but cannot do ranges.
Breaking text into terms, the first step in building a searchable inverted index.
Normalizing tokens, such as lowercasing and reducing words to a root, so related words match.
The inverted index one shard keeps over its own documents, queried in parallel with the others.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: A query often filters on several columns, and the order of columns in a composite index matters. An index on (customer, date) helps a query that filters by customer, or by customer and date, but not one that filters by date alone, because the index is sorted by customer first. Getting this order wrong is why an index that looks relevant is never used [[pg-indexes-multicolumn]].

The database does not use an index just because one exists; the query planner decides. If a condition matches most of the table, a scan can be cheaper than jumping through an index row by row, so the planner may ignore the index on purpose. Reading the chosen plan is how you learn whether your index is actually helping [[pg-indexes-intro]].

Search ranks rather than just matches. Once the inverted index finds the documents containing the query terms, the engine scores them, so the most relevant come first. Classic scoring weighs how often a term appears in a document against how common it is across all documents, so a rare, on-topic word counts for more than a common one [[lucene]].

terms.definition: An index over several columns; the column order decides which queries it can serve.
A composite index helps queries that use its first columns, not ones that skip them.
Answering a query from the index alone, without touching the table, when the index holds every needed column.
Ranking matching documents so the most relevant appear first.
Scoring that rewards a term appearing often in a document but being rare across all documents.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Every index is a bet: it speeds some queries while slowing all writes and taking space. The practical discipline is to index for the queries you actually run, confirm with the query plan that each index is used, and drop ones that are not. An unused index is pure cost. PostgreSQL devotes a whole section to examining whether your indexes are being used and refining them against the real workload [[pg-indexes-examine]].

Databases and search engines make opposite default bargains. A relational B-tree index favours exact and range lookups on structured columns and strong consistency; a search engine favours flexible text matching and ranking, often updating its index slightly behind the source data. Many systems use both: the database as the source of truth, a search index kept in sync beside it [[es-docs]].

At scale the two topics meet. A sharded database spreads rows across shards, and a search cluster spreads its inverted index across shards the same way, running each query on every shard and merging results. The indexing ideas here are what make queries fast within each shard, so this topic completes the data path the earlier topics built [[es-docs]].

misconceptions.myth: More indexes always make a database faster.
misconceptions.truth: Each index slows every write and takes space; only indexes the planner actually uses help [[pg-indexes-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: An index on the right column is always used.
misconceptions.truth: The planner may skip it when a scan is cheaper, and a composite index helps only its leftmost columns [[pg-indexes-multicolumn]].

misconceptions.myth: Full-text search is just a LIKE query on steroids.
misconceptions.truth: It builds an inverted index with tokenization and analysis, then ranks matches by relevance [[lucene]].

misconceptions.myth: A search index is always perfectly in sync with the database.
misconceptions.truth: It is often near-real-time, reflecting new data after a short delay, so it can trail the source [[es-docs]].
